originalTitle: Now, Autonomy by Max Easton review – a sardonic yet compassionate take on millennial apathy
summary: The author’s third novel to chronicle life in Sydney’s west follows a group of flawed friends trying to sustain meaning amid an ‘erosion in the world’
content: If any part of Australia can lay claim to being the country’s literary nexus, it is western Sydney. The wide wing of suburbia is both home to and the subject of granular attention for an ever-growing list of acclaimed writers: Yumna Kassab, Peter Polites, Luke Carman, Michael Mohammed Ahmad, Felicity Castagna – to name just a few. Each of them reflects a culturally diverse landscape in which social class and suburban identity are forever intersecting, animating the lives of those often neglected in the margins of Australia’s projected self-image. A key figure in this discourse is Max Easton, whose latest novel – Now, Autonomy – is the third instalment of his multi-decade series that chronicles working-class struggle and its subcultural undercurrents in Sydney’s west. Beginning with the Miles Franklin-longlisted The Magpie Wing in 2021, and followed by Paradise Estate in 2023, this ambitious, compelling quasi-trilogy – each title can be read and appreciated on its own – depicts people navigating Australia’s class hierarchies, hyper-gentrification, rental housing pressures and ever-diminishing spaces for community and collective activism. We continue as Easton started, thrown into an ecosystem of progressively minded, albeit flawed, friends trying to sustain a meaningful existence. The shrewd Helen Coleman, who started as a teenager in The Magpie Wing, is now in her late 30s. Among her friends these days is her reclusive flatmate Pat, a middle-aged sound guy who can’t seem to shake the past; her off-kilter former housemate Sunny, whose restlessness for radical change is as irksome as it is imperative; Sunny’s partner, Sio, the only one of them with a somewhat put-together life; and Helen’s partner, Maria, who is caring yet increasingly despondent amid the holding pattern of their relationship. Everyone is varyingly disillusioned and struggling to reorient themselves while fending off financial insecurity, creative inertia and interpersonal disaffection. Helen senses an “erosion in the world”: Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues unabated despite global protest, the economic gulfs of the 21st century are becoming yawning chasms and the commodification of artistic expression is even infecting the DIY scenes that sprang up in opposition to it. Collectively, there is a psychic strain: everyone cares for each other but is also exhausted by the emotional labour; everyone is quick to speculate about other people’s problems yet uninterested in addressing their own. When not numbed before this “great defeat”, the gang seek to reorient themselves around a sense of agency and purpose. Reclamation of autonomy – personal and collective – is the novel’s focal point, as is the tension in doing so meaningfully. When everyone haphazardly tries to set up a new music venue called The Quarterly, it’s unclear how much it’s really to save “Sydney from itself” or themselves from the void. When that ambition is cut short and as fragments of Pat’s activist history are unearthed, a more radical project emerges. But what is really motivating each person? And is being part of an insignificant attempt at change itself still significant? Now, Autonomy may sound like a jaded novel – but though it holds a mirror to cynicism, it is far from cynical itself. Indeed, it is a deeply compassionate work, more interested in diagnosing the causes of apathy than deriding it. As Easton has said, a driving motivation for him has been to address his fellow millennials who “bemoan the city and cultural milieu we’ve been handed without realising we’re not providing much more to those who come after us”. His writing is acerbic and sardonically funny while reflecting this, and is palpably alive to the strains of contemporary life while striving to give a voice to the means of resistance. In a similar vein to what Emmett Stinson pointed out in The Magpie Wing, there are occasions in Now, Autonomy when Easton overtly expounds a point, as if intent on eschewing subtext. For example, when Pat is describing a certain condemned building to Sunny: “Everything is rotting in there. I dunno, I guess everything’s rotting now. The only things doing well are the things that feed on rot. Real estate. Banks. Internet.” Message received. Whether intentional or not, amid what is otherwise a novel of richly rendered place and nuanced characters, these moments at best flatten things and at worst dislodge you from the narrative. But as a whole, Easton’s newest addition to his remarkable tapestry of western Sydney is tantalisingly alive. It is an ode to people who reach towards change – even in ways conceited or delusional – as they struggle to get by in a world increasingly resistant to accommodating them. You fall effortlessly into their lives and find yourself in them. For that Now, Autonomy should be applauded. Now, Autonomy by Max Easton is out now (Giramondo, A$32.95)
chineseTitle: 现在，马克斯·伊斯顿的《Autonomy》评论——对千禧一代的冷漠态度进行了讽刺而富有同情心的呈现
chineseSummary: 作者的第三部记录悉尼西部生活的小说讲述了一群有缺陷的朋友试图在“世界的侵蚀”中维持意义的故事
chineseContent: 如果说澳大利亚有哪个地方可以称得上是该国的文学中心的话，那就是悉尼西部了。郊区的宽阔翼区既是越来越多的著名作家的故乡，也是他们关注的主题：Yumna Kassab、Peter Polites、Luke Carman、Michael Mohammed Ahmad、Felicity Castagna 等，仅举几例。它们每一个都反映了多元文化的景观，其中社会阶层和郊区身份永远交叉，为那些经常被澳大利亚自我形象边缘忽视的人们的生活注入活力。这一论述中的关键人物是马克斯·伊斯顿（Max Easton），他的最新小说《现在，自治》是他数十年系列小说的第三部分，该系列记录了悉尼西部工人阶级的斗争及其亚文化暗流。从 2021 年入围迈尔斯·富兰克林入围名单的《喜鹊之翼》开始，到 2023 年的《天堂庄园》，这部雄心勃勃、引人入胜的准三部曲——每部作品都可以单独阅读和欣赏——描绘了人们在澳大利亚的阶级等级、过度中产阶级化、租房压力以及社区和集体活动空间不断缩小的过程中的处境。我们继续像伊斯顿一样开始，被扔进一个思想进步的生态系统，尽管有缺陷，朋友们试图维持有意义的存在。精明的海伦·科尔曼 (Helen Coleman) 十几岁时就加入了喜鹊之翼，现在已经 30 多岁了。这些天她的朋友中有她隐居的室友帕特，一个中年健全的人，似乎无法摆脱过去。她的前室友桑尼（Sunny）格格不入，他对彻底改变的焦躁不安既令人厌烦，又势在必行； Sunny 的伴侣 Sio，是他们中唯一一个生活还算是井然有序的人。海伦的伴侣玛丽亚虽然很关心，但在等待的过程中却越来越沮丧
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
